name: Metronidazole / ivermectin (rosacea creams)

lead: Topical metronidazole and ivermectin 1% cream (Soolantra) are prescription treatments for the inflammatory bumps of rosacea, aimed at a clearer, calmer complexion. They mainly reduce inflamed lesions and redness around them, and do little for persistent flat facial redness, which vasoconstrictors and lasers target instead.

Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial; its benefit in rosacea may come from antibacterial or anti-inflammatory action. Ivermectin acts on invertebrate parasites, and its use rests on the idea that Demodex mites contribute to rosacea. Rosacea overviews describe topical metronidazole as having good evidence for reducing inflammatory bumps; in one cited study ivermectin reduced lesions by 83% over four months versus 74% for metronidazole.

paras: Both are applied to the face as a cream or gel as part of a daily routine prescribed by a clinician, often alongside gentle cleansing and sunscreen. Rosacea overviews describe them as treatments for the inflammatory form, and people combine them with other products when persistent redness is also a concern.

Topical use commonly causes mild local redness, dryness, burning or itching, especially early. Oral metronidazole carries an FDA boxed warning about carcinogenicity in rodents, which applies to the systemic drug, not the topical product. Both topicals require a prescription in the US.

angle.text: Prescription metronidazole and ivermectin creams calm the bumps and inflammation of rosacea, leaving a clearer, less irritated face. They work by settling inflammation rather than shrinking vessels, so they do little for persistent flat redness. Both are well described in rosacea overviews for the bump-type condition.

lead: Topical metronidazole and topical ivermectin are two prescription creams or gels used for the inflammatory form of rosacea. Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial developed by Rhône-Poulenc and first marketed in France in 1960 [1][2]. Ivermectin was discovered through work by Satoshi Ōmura and William Campbell, who shared part of the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it, and the 1% cream is sold as Soolantra for rosacea [3].

Rosacea overviews describe topical metronidazole as having good evidence for reducing inflammatory bumps and redness around lesions, while doing little for persistent facial redness [4]. In one clinical study cited there, ivermectin reduced lesions by 83% over four months versus 74% for metronidazole, and a review found it more effective than alternatives for papulopustular rosacea [4].
Both are prescription-only in the US, UK and Canada for metronidazole [2].
infobox: Inflammatory papules and pustules of rosacea

paras: Topical rosacea treatments are used for papules and pustules, with separate options such as brimonidine and oxymetazoline directed at persistent redness [4]. Topical metronidazole is among the established options, with several studies reporting benefit even though the mechanism is not well understood [2][4]. Ivermectin is used for the same inflammatory lesions on the premise that Demodex mites contribute to rosacea, and regulators in the US and Europe have approved it for inflammatory lesions [4].

Rosacea overviews state that topical metronidazole reduces inflammatory lesions and perilesional redness and is generally well tolerated, though it does little for persistent facial redness [4]. Ivermectin cream outperformed metronidazole in the study cited there (83% versus 74% lesion reduction at four months) [4]. Because these treatments act on lesions, those seeking to reduce background redness are often described as using vasoconstrictors or vascular lasers instead [4].

Topical metronidazole commonly causes local redness, dryness and irritation, and tearing if applied near the eyes [2]. Ivermectin cream can cause transient burning or itching [4]. Most topical rosacea options cause local irritation early in treatment [4].

The FDA label for oral metronidazole carries a boxed warning noting carcinogenicity in mice and rats and advising against unnecessary use; it also lists seizures, neuropathy and severe cutaneous adverse reactions as systemic risks [5]. That label concerns the oral drug, not the topical rosacea products.

Metronidazole is a prodrug reduced in anaerobic organisms to a radical that damages DNA; this activation needs low oxygen, so it has little effect on human cells or aerobic bacteria [2]. Ivermectin binds glutamate-gated chloride channels in invertebrate nerve and muscle cells, paralysing the parasite; mammals are largely protected because it does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier [3].

Rhône-Poulenc developed metronidazole in the 1950s; commercial use began in France in 1960 and Searle later licensed it [1][2]. Ōmura isolated Streptomyces avermitilis from Japanese soil in 1970, Campbell's group at Merck developed ivermectin, and it was marketed as a veterinary product from 1981 and approved for human use in 1987 [3].

The rosacea-specific head-to-head figure above comes from a secondary overview [4]. The registered metronidazole trials in the available record concern other indications such as bacterial vaginosis, periodontal disease, C. difficile and leishmaniasis [6][7][8][9], not rosacea. Detailed rosacea trial reports for both creams are not summarised here.
The creams are mentioned in skincare circles as dermatologist-prescribed options for rosacea bumps, usually distinguished from products that target flat background redness.
